messages:
maria: quick question — auth precedence for the CLI when we have multiple sources: REDWOOD_API_KEY in env, --profile flag, ~/.redwood/config profiles, OS keyring entries, and tokens injected by an external vault agent. what order does the CLI use, and what’s the recommended fallback pattern for scripts (esp in CI)? also seeing streaming output get buffered when piping — any known quirks?

jason: short answer: env vars should win (explicit), then CLI flags, then profile in config, then OS keyring, then interactive helpers/askpass. external vault-injected env tokens are fine — treat them like env vars. for CI, avoid interactive helpers.

priya: concrete bash snippet that’s worked for us (keeps noninteractive, tries env then config then keyring):

```bash
get_redwood_token() {
  [[ -n \"$REDWOOD_API_KEY\" ]] && { printf '%s' "$REDWOOD_API_KEY"; return; }
  [[ -n \"$1\" ]] && { redwood auth use --profile "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 && redwood auth export-token --profile "$1"; return; }
  # try config default profile
  cfg_profile=$(redwood config get default_profile || true)
  [[ -n \"$cfg_profile\" ]] && { redwood auth export-token --profile "$cfg_profile"; return; }
  # OS keyring (linux example using secret-tool)
  if command -v secret-tool >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    secret-tool lookup redwood token || true
  fi
}

# usage: TOKEN=$(get_redwood_token my-profile)
# streaming note: force line buffering if piping: `stdbuf -oL redwood chat --stream ...`
```

sam: Windows PowerShell variant (use for CI on windows):

```powershell
function Get-RedwoodToken {
  param([string]$Profile)
  if ($env:REDWOOD_API_KEY) { return $env:REDWOOD_API_KEY }
  if ($Profile) { return (redwood auth export-token --profile $Profile) }
  # try config
  $cfg = redwood config get default_profile 2>$null
  if ($cfg) { return (redwood auth export-token --profile $cfg) }
  # Windows Credential Manager (example using PowerShell-CredentialStore module)
  try { return (Get-StoredCredential -Target 'redwood' -ErrorAction Stop).Password } catch { return $null }
}
# note: PowerShell may buffer stdout; use `--stream` and call redwood directly in console when you need live output.
```

jason: small addendum on askpass: the CLI may fall back to an askpass helper if no noninteractive credentials are found. that breaks CI. best practices: set REDWOOD_API_KEY in CI, or mount a small file and `export REDWOOD_API_KEY=$(cat /secrets/redwood_token)` during job setup. if you control the runner, prefer short-lived tokens from your vault agent injected as env vars.

priya: streaming buffering specifics we ran into: when you pipe CLI output into another process (eg `redwood chat --stream ... | jq .`), standard C stdio buffering can delay bytes. two workarounds: `stdbuf -oL` (linux) or `unbuffer` from expect. on docker images use `--output-pty` for the CLI (if available) so it uses line-buffering. also the SDK/websocket path avoids this buffering entirely.

maria: thanks — one follow-up: any gotchas with WSL and keyrings? we have devs on wsl2 who expect credential sync w/ Windows keychain.

sam: WSL is annoying: gnome-keyring/secret-service inside distro is separate from Windows Credential Manager. recommended: for WSL devs either store in file under ~/.redwood and protect perms, or run a small helper on Windows that writes token to a file accessible to WSL via /mnt/c/..., then use the bash function to read it. avoid relying on `secret-tool` cross-platform.

ci-bot: FYI: vault tokens injected into CI rotate every 6h — make sure your token refresh path can re-read env or file each job run. :rotating_light:

maria: great, this is enough to prototype. i'll add a `scripts/get-token.{sh,ps1}` to repo and update our CI to export REDWOOD_API_KEY from the vault agent. thanks all :thumbsup:
